claims.text: Wear performance improves as ambient temperature rises from 25 °C to approximately 600–700 °C.
Moderate temperatures promote formation of a dense, self-healing oxide layer.
Moderate temperatures promote dynamic recrystallization in the coating.
Self-healing oxide formation and dynamic recrystallization reduce friction and wear.
Wear rate increases sharply above approximately 700 °C.
High-temperature phase instability contributes to degradation of the coating.
An HEA was observed to undergo phase instability at 700 °C after 1000 hours.
TiO can transform from an elevated-temperature FCC structure to a monoclinic structure at ambient temperature.
Complex oxides such as TiNb2O7 can be non-protective in a B2-strengthened refractory HEA.
Protective Cr2O3 formation is composition- and condition-dependent, and it may be absent during high-temperature oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between a coating and metallic substrate can produce interfacial cracking during cooling.
Thermal-expansion-mismatch cracking accelerates tribological wear in the proposed HEA coating system.
Phase instability produces brittle, unprotective oxides and loss of mechanical strength, thereby accelerating wear.
The initial coating may possess a metastable single-phase or dual-phase BCC/B2 microstructure.
Reciprocating wear behavior of an HEA has been investigated under atmospheric conditions from ambient temperature to 900 °C.
An exposure of approximately 100 hours or equivalent wear cycles is sufficient to form the relevant oxide scales.
The wear-rate response is non-monotonic, with a minimum near 600–700 °C followed by degradation.
The critical degradation boundary lies between 600 °C and 900 °C.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis and predicted outcome place the transition near 600–700 °C or above 700 °C, whereas the boundary field broadens it to 600–900 °C, leaving the proposed cutoff internally inconsistent.

The mechanism allows phase instability or loss of strength to increase wear independently of oxide-scale failure, but the falsification rule treats an adherent protective scale during increased wear as falsifying the entire hypothesis even if phase instability is observed.
